title: Redwood edgecases demo: long context + high TPS + streaming backpressure/timeouts
summary: Redwood walked Nimbus through an edge-cases demo focusing on long-context handling (~100k tokens), high TPS load patterns, streaming backpressure behavior and timeout/retry strategies. Discussed tradeoffs (latency vs cost), Dedicated vs Hosted, VPC/KMS, and next steps for a 48h POC and security docs. Action items and follow-ups agreed.

transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-02-20
Time: 14:00 PT
Duration: ~62 minutes
Attendees: Samir Patel (Redwood AE), Jin Park (Redwood SE), Maya Lopez (Nimbus CTO), Evan Chen (Nimbus SRE), Priya Rao (Nimbus Eng Manager)

Auto-summary (auto-gen, may be incomplete): Walkthrough of edge-case behavior w/ long contexts, high TPS, streaming backpressure. Demo included simulated load and streaming chunking. Discussed Dedicated vs Hosted and security.

[00:00] Samir: Hey everyone, thanks for joining. I'm Samir from Redwood, AE on this account. With me is Jin our SE. Today we're going to demo a couple of edge cases you flagged — long context, high throughput day, and streaming backpressure and timeout behaviors.

[00:25] Maya: Thanks, Samir. We care a lot about long context — some of our agents need to reference multi-session logs, like 80k-120k token histories. Also the SRE team wants to know how streaming holds up under load, and what happens when clients hit timeouts.

[00:45] Jin: Great, yeah, we'll start with how Redwood manages long context and memory, then move into throughput tests. Quick note — in the demo environment we'll emulate a 100k token prefix and then drive varying TPS.

[01:12] Evan: Quick qual: are you using Hosted or Dedicated in the test infra? We have different network constraints and some internal security folks are picky about VPCs.

[01:25] Samir: For the demo we're running on a Dedicated-like cluster in our lab with VPC networking enabled to mirror your set-up. It's not customer data, but the config is equivalent. We'll point out config bits for Hosted vs Dedicated.

[02:00] Jin: All right, jumping in — long context. At a high level we do prefix KV caching, chunked attention with windowing, and model variants with longer position embeddings. For very long sequences we avoid reprocessing the whole prefix every request by maintaining a KV cache keyed by chat/session id.

[02:37] Maya: Sorry, you said KV cash?

[02:40] Jin: (laughs) KV cache, yes — sometimes the transcript gets it as cash.

[03:05] Jin: So what that looks like in practice: initial ingest of a 100k token trace will take longer (higher latency on that first request) but subsequent queries that reference the same prefix reuse KV state and are much faster. Batching and continuous KV reuse brings down per-token compute.

[03:45] Priya: What's the memory footprint for a 100k prefix? We're thinking about GPU memory on T4 vs A100; quantized models too.

[04:00] Jin: Good question. Memory is roughly proportional to sequence length and model size. With 8-bit quant quantization+memory optimizations we observed X GB per 100k tokens on our 70B family — (note: the number here is an example in demo, we'll provide exact bench sheet). For A100-class hardware you have a lot more headroom; on smaller cards you can shard across GPUs.

[04:34] Evan: How about fallbacks if the model can't accept a 100k prefix? Do you auto-trim or use a summarization step?

[04:45] Jin: We have policies. You can configure automatic prefix summarization, ring-buffer trimming, or reroute to a model variant with extended context. For POC we'd recommend a combination: keep most recent N tokens and run periodic summarization of older segments.

[05:10] Samir: Moving on to high TPS. We ran a synthetic test at varying TPS up to 2k TPS for short completions. Two levers: batching and routing. Batching increases compute efficiency but raises p99 latency; routing can send traffic to lower-cost model variants or Dedicated capacity.

[06:00] Maya: Realistically we expect bursty traffic — 1k sustained with spikes to 3k for a few minutes. How do you handle autoscaling?

[06:15] Jin: Autoscaling leverages queue depth and target latency. We maintain a small warm pool and scale GPU nodes with burst credit. For Dedicated you can set reserved capacity. There are tradeoffs: scaling fast reduces queued requests but comes at cost.

[06:40] Evan: Do you do prewarm or cold-start mitigation for model loads?

[06:50] Jin: Yes — model preloading and pinned replicas for hot routes. Also granular route-level SLOs so the most critical routes have lower queue thresholds.

[07:30] Samir: Now streaming backpressure — we'll demo a streaming session where client-side imposes a 200ms read timeout and then recovers.

[07:45] (screen shared)

[08:05] Jin: We start a streaming response with chunked tokens. At normal conditions tokens flow, but when the client simulates a slow consumer the server's outgoing buffer fills and we apply backpressure; Redwood's runtime can either pause generation or continue and buffer up to a configured limit.

[08:35] Maya: What happens at buffer limit? Do you drop connections or throttle?

[08:40] Jin: Configurable. Options: 1) apply backpressure to slow producers (pause token generation), 2) buffer up to N MB and then signal an error to client, or 3) fall back to non-streaming (return a final chunk). For mission critical you typically pause generation and extend server-side timeouts.

[09:05] Evan: And client reconnection? Any conversation idempotency guarantees?

[09:20] Jin: We provide idempotency tokens and resume semantics. If a client reconnects with the same id and last received token index, the server can resume or retransmit the remainder. That requires the client to persist last-seen index.

[10:00] Priya: Timeout policies — what should our client set for read and overall request timeouts?

[10:12] Samir: Depends on latency SLOs. For streaming, recommend a short read timeout for interactive UI (200-500ms) but a longer overall request timeout for long generation when you expect stalls (30-60s). For non-interactive batch jobs, use longer timeouts or non-streaming calls.

[10:50] (demo: simulate client slow read at 500ms, then at 2s, then client reconnect)

[12:00] Jin: Observed behavior: at 500ms pause, the runtime paused generation after buffer built up; client resumed and we picked up. At 2s the buffer hit threshold and we switched to final-chunk fallback and signaled a 504 to client. This is why we recommend a client backoff and resume flow.

[12:40] Maya: Does Redwood expose metrics for buffer fill/streaming backpressure so our SREs can alert?

[12:55] Jin: Yes — in Console you get per-route metrics: streaming buffer utilization, stream disconnect rates, per-token latency, and per-connection queue depth. You can set alerts on those metrics.

[13:30] Evan: I'm concerned about timeouts under heavy load and how retried requests affect billing and downstream duplicates.

[13:45] Samir: Great point. Retries can double bill if you resubmit the same generation. We recommend idempotency tokens and server-side dedupe where applicable. Also Redwood Optimize suggests caching at prefix-level to reduce re-compute on retries.

[14:12] Priya: Any demo of a real POC workload?

[14:20] Jin: Yes — we have a sample POC playbook. For your case we'd run a 48h baseline: replay your traffic at scale (1k sustained, spikes to 3k) with prefixes sampled from your corpus (we need your replay file). We'll measure p50/p95 latency, errors, cost per 1M tokens, and KV cache hit rates.

[15:05] Maya: About security — we need SOC2 and SSO. Also how KMS is used for keys?

[15:20] Samir: We'll share SOC2 report and our security whitepaper. For customer-managed keys, Dedicated and Private support KMS/HSM integrations; we can provide guidance on rotating keys and audit logs.

[15:40] Evan: Data residency — any options?

[15:45] Samir: Hosted has region controls; Dedicated can be provisioned in specific cloud regions; Private/on-prem is an option for strict residency requirements.

[16:10] (demo continues: live measurement graphs showing p95 latency vs TPS, streaming disconnects)

[18:00] Jin: One thing we emphasize — quality vs cost. For high TPS you may route to smaller quantized models for non-critical routes. For critical flows use larger models pinned to Dedicated capacity. Redwood Optimize gives recommendations automatically based on eval sets.

[19:05] Maya: Can Optimize auto-suggest quantization profiles?

[19:15] Jin: Yes — it analyses your workload and suggests quantization and batching configs with estimated cost/quality deltas. We'll include sample output for your workload.

[20:00] (customer asks about competitor behavior)

[20:10] Maya: How is this different from running on Vertex or just OpenAI?

[20:20] Samir: The differentiator is production control: unified runtime across Hosted/Dedicated/Private, per-route SLOs, KV caching, and cost-aware routing. Also our Console and Optimize tools give granular cost/quality tradeoffs aligned to engineering workflows.

[21:05] Evan: Ok let's talk POC specifics — what do you need from us?

[21:20] Jin: We'll need your workload replay (har or protobuf), a list of critical routes, target SLOs, and a contact for infra access. We'll provision a POC cluster and run 48h test.

[22:00] Samir: I'll own the POC coordination and send the benchmark template and pricing. Jin will provide the deployment config and POC steps.

[22:15] Priya: On billing during POC — will we be charged?

[22:25] Samir: POCs typically have a trial credit; if you opt for Dedicated reserved capacity there may be a short-term commit. We'll outline options in pricing.

[23:00] (toward wrap)

[23:10] Maya: A couple of last clarifying q's — if our client timeouts cause partial streams, is there tooling to reconcile partial outputs back to a single canonical response?

[23:30] Jin: The resume semantics + idempotency helps; additionally you can do final-chunk retrieval after streaming to ensure a canonical output is stored. For mission-critical flows you might prefer synchronous non-streaming calls to avoid partials.

[24:00] Evan: For cost analysis, we'd like per-route token cost at both p50 and p95 latencies.

[24:10] Samir: Yep, Console exposes token-level cost breakdown per route and model. Optimize can give you projected cost for different quant/model choices.

[25:00] (silence, folks skim shared docs)

[25:30] Samir: Recap and next steps — we'll send benchmark spreadsheet, SOC2 report, POC playbook, and a proposed calendar invite for a POC kickoff next week. Jin will attach the config snippets. Evan, you to share workload replay.

[25:55] Maya: Sounds good. A timing ask: can we kick off POC by end of next week?

[26:05] Samir: Yes, we can try to start by 2026-02-26 if we get the replay this week.

[26:20] Priya: Also please include a note on expected GPU types and memory requirements so infra can provision.

[26:30] Jin: Will do.

[26:45] (small crosstalk)

[27:00] Samir: Any other questions?

[27:05] Evan: Not from me.

[27:10] Maya: All good. Thank you both.

[27:20] Samir: Thanks everyone. We'll follow up with the docs and invite.

[27:30] (call ends)
